issues.item: Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
issues.explanation: The trigger set leans strongly toward direct combat/attack cues (suspicious people, gunshot noise), which is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of trauma to a loved one unless the loved one’s trauma specifically occurred in a combat or shooting context. As written, these triggers suggest personal threat exposure more than reminders of harm to a loved one.

The appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies prominent moral injury/self-blame for one’s own actions. That can occur after trauma to a loved one, but here there are no corresponding memory details or other appraisals linking the loved one’s trauma to the patient’s own actions/omissions. In this profile it pulls toward a different trauma meaning than the rest of the items and is not well supported by the selected trigger and memory content.

For trauma to a loved one, gunshot noise as a prominent trigger is hard to reconcile unless the loved one's trauma specifically involved gunfire. Nothing in the rest of the profile supports a gunfire/combat-linked bereavement context, so this trigger appears trauma-context mismatched.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies morally injurious personal action during the event. That is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one unless there is additional context about the patient's own actions. The rest of the profile centers on loss, mistrust, and intrusive recall rather than perpetration-related guilt, making this item stand out as clinically incoherent.

vignette:
Anjali had always found a sense of order in the cockpit, a place where procedure and skill could master chaos. For six months, however, that order has been shattered. The trauma was not to her, but to her wingman, Ben, and she had a perfect, front-row seat. It was a routine training exercise, a high-G turn over the desert, when his engine failed catastrophically. There was no time for an ejection. Anjali watched his F-16 fall from the sky, a silent, sickening arc that ended in a plume of black smoke against the sand. She circled the wreckage, her own radio calls unanswered, feeling the oppressive heat of the sun through the canopy and the tight, useless grip of her harness.

In the weeks that followed, the cockpit, once her sanctuary, became a source of torment. The simple act of strapping in and feeling the familiar discomfort of her flight suit would instantly trigger the memory of that day. It wasn't a thought, but a full sensory replay; her mind would project the memory onto the back of her eyes like a film that plays over and over, complete with the silence on the radio and the stark, photographic image of the smoke against the horizon. To escape this, Anjali began trying desperately to push the images away. She would try hard not to think about the trauma, focusing with ferocious intensity on pre-flight checklists or the hum of the avionics, believing she could wall off the memory through sheer force of will.

This strategy consistently failed. The more she tried to suppress the images, the more powerfully they would return, ambushing her without warning. The effort of suppression also reinforced a terrifying new belief: that there was something fundamentally wrong with her. Her inability to control her own mind felt like a deep personal defect. This appraisal became a constant, humming background to her days. While she sat in briefings, she was no longer just a pilot among her peers; she was the broken one, the one who couldn't cope. This conviction that she was defective made the memories feel deserved, almost like a punishment she had to endure, and they would surface with even greater clarity and frequency.

The triggers began to multiply, fed by the vividness of the memories themselves. Having relived the crash so many times, she became exquisitely sensitive to anything that echoed it. A conversation in the mess hall about a civilian plane crash or someone mentioning a friend who had lost a loved one would feel like a direct physical blow. These discussions didn't just remind her of Ben; they activated a profound sense of guilt. She would be certain in those moments that she should have protected him, that she had failed in her most basic duty as a wingman. This belief, in turn, would drag the memory of the falling jet back to the forefront of her mind, each recollection solidifying her sense of failure.

Her avoidance expanded beyond her own thoughts. She started actively steering clear of her squadron mates, especially those who wanted to talk about Ben or ask how she was doing. Being reminded of the event by others felt unbearable, so she ate alone and spent her free time in her room. This isolation had a corrosive effect on her self-perception. In her solitude, the belief that she couldn't rely on other people began to take root, morphing into a certainty that she was unworthy of their support anyway. She stopped initiating contact and began declining invitations, effectively cutting herself off. This withdrawal fed her conviction that she was defective, creating a closed loop of self-blame and isolation. She has not even considered starting a new friendship or relationship, certain that she would only fail or contaminate anyone who got too close.

Anjali is now in therapy not by choice, but because her commanding officer noticed her sharp decline in flight performance and her stark withdrawal from the squadron. She was grounded pending a psychological evaluation. What frightens her most is not the memory itself, but the conclusion it has led her to: that the disciplined, capable pilot she once was is gone forever, replaced by someone broken, unreliable, and fundamentally flawed. She is terrified that she will never fly again, and that she has already failed the last person she can—herself.
